title: DSA in Java: arrays and hashing
seriesDescription: Hashing, windows, stacks, binary search, lists, trees, heaps and graphs with Java code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Java hashing for interviews: HashMap idioms (merge, computeIfAbsent), equals/hashCode, prefix sums, anagram grouping and expected versus worst-case cost.
source: Oracle Java documentation (HashMap, Map.merge, Integer cache, Arrays.sort); LeetCode two sum, group anagrams and subarray sum equals K; Cracking the Coding Interview

questions.prompt: Write a Java method `int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target)` that returns the indices of two different elements adding up to target in one pass using a `HashMap` (assume exactly one answer exists).
questions.starter:
static int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
  
}

checks.label: uses a HashMap/Map from value to index
looks up the complement target - nums[i]
checks the map with get or containsKey

questions.explanation: Check the map before inserting the current element, otherwise `nums = {3, 2, 4}` with `target 6` pairs index 0 with itself. Other correct solutions (`containsKey`, a fill-first pass) also pass.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method `Collection<List<String>> groupAnagrams(String[] words)` that groups words that are anagrams of each other, using a `Map` keyed by the word's sorted letters.

checks.label: sorts the characters of each word
turns the sorted letters back into a String key
appends each word to its group

questions.explanation: `Arrays.sort` works on a `char[]` and `new String(char[])` rebuilds a hashable key. A 26-slot count array turned into a string such as `"1#0#2..."` also works and avoids the k log k sort.

questions.prompt: Write a Java method `int subarraySum(int[] nums, int k)` that counts the contiguous subarrays whose sum equals `k`. The array may contain negative numbers, so aim for O(n) with a `HashMap` of prefix sums.
questions.starter:
static int subarraySum(int[] nums, int k) {
  
}

checks.label: uses a map from prefix sum to how often it occurred
seeds the map with prefix 0 occurring once

questions.explanation: Because values can be negative a sliding window does not work. Counting before recording the current prefix keeps a zero-length subarray from being counted. Overflow is possible with huge values; use `long` if the constraints say so.

questions.prompt: Match each Java Map call with what it does.

right.text: Adds one to the stored count, inserting 1 when the key is missing
Reads the value, or 0 when the key is missing, without inserting anything
Creates and stores a value when the key is missing, then returns the value for k
Stores v only when the key has no mapping, returning the old value if there was one
Deletes the mapping and returns the previous value or `null`
Locks the entry so other threads cannot touch it

questions.explanation: `merge` counts in one call, `computeIfAbsent` builds multi-maps, `getOrDefault` avoids a null check, and `putIfAbsent` keeps the first value. These four replace most `containsKey`-then-put code in interview solutions.

questions.text: To count with a HashMap, call map.{1}(key, 1, Integer::{2}); to group values by key, call map.{3}(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(value).
questions.explanation: merge with Integer::sum inserts 1 for a new key and adds 1 for an existing one. computeIfAbsent returns the list, so you can chain add on it.

questions.prompt: A default `new HashMap<>()` has 16 buckets and a load factor of 0.75. Before inserting a new entry would trigger the first resize, what is the largest number of entries it can hold?
questions.explanation: `16 x 0.75 = 12`. The threshold is exceeded by the 13th insertion, which doubles the table to 32 buckets and rehashes. Pass an initial capacity (about expectedSize / 0.75 + 1) when you know the size up front.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: A `HashMap`-based two sum is guaranteed O(n) time even in the worst case.
questions.reason: `HashMap get and put` take O(1) time on average.

whys.a: A is not true as stated, so no explanation can hold.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are out.
whys.c: R is true, so option c cannot hold.
whys.d: Correct: O(1) is an average-case (expected) bound. With many collisions, treeified bins cost O(log n) per lookup for Comparable keys, so the worst case is not O(n).

questions.explanation: Say "expected O(n)" in an interview. It shows you know the difference between expected and worst-case hash costs.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Grouping anagrams by `Arrays.sort` on each word's char array costs O(n * k log k) for n words of length k.
questions.reason: Sorting the k characters of one word takes O(k) time.

whys.a: R is false, so this cannot be right.
whys.b: R is false, so no both-true option holds.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (n sorts of cost k log k) but comparison sorting k characters takes O(k log k), not O(k).
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: The alternative key is a 26-count signature, giving O(n * k) for lowercase words. Mention both.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: If a field used by `hashCode` is changed after an object was added to a `HashSet`, `contains` may no longer find it.
questions.reason: The bucket for an element is chosen from its `hashCode` at the moment it is inserted.

whys.a: Correct: the entry stays in the old bucket while lookups go to the new bucket, so the object is effectively lost.
whys.b: R is exactly why the lookup fails, so it does explain A.
whys.c: R is true, so c is wrong.
whys.d: A is true, so d is wrong.

questions.explanation: Use immutable fields (or records) in keys. This is also why mutable lists make poor map keys.

questions.prompt: A Java class overrides `equals` but not `hashCode`, and instances are stored in a `HashSet`. What can go wrong?

options.text: Equal objects can land in different buckets, so `contains` may fail.
options.why: Correct: the default `hashCode` is identity based, so two equal objects usually hash to different buckets.

options.text: The class fails to compile, because the compiler insists both methods are overridden together.
options.why: The compiler only warns in some tools; it does not enforce the pair.

options.text: The set throws an exception on the second `add` of an object equal to an existing one.
options.why: Sets silently ignore duplicates; they never throw for them.

options.text: The set switches to comparing by identity for every later call to `add` or `contains`.
options.why: The set keeps using `hashCode` and `equals`; nothing switches mode at run time.

questions.explanation: Also never use a mutable field in `hashCode` for keys you keep in a map. `Objects.hash(...)` and records give a correct pair for free.

questions.prompt: This Java two sum puts first and then checks: `for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) { seen.put(nums[i], i); Integer j = seen.get(target - nums[i]); if (j != null) return new int[]{j, i}; }`. What does it return for `nums = {3, 2, 4}`, `target = 6`?

options.why: That needs the lookup to run before the put; this order never gets there.

options.text: An empty array, because no pair sums to 6
options.why: The pair 2 and 4 exists, and the loop returns earlier anyway.

options.text: A NullPointerException on the first iteration
options.why: get returns null for a missing key, and the code compares j with null first.
Correct: after putting 3 at index 0 the lookup of 6 - 3 finds index 0 straight away.

questions.explanation: Look up the complement before storing the current value. This is the classic "use the same element twice" bug. I ran it: the result is {0, 0}.

questions.prompt: With `Integer a = 1000, b = 1000` (boxed values), `a == b` is false in standard Java, so values read from a `Map<Integer, Integer>` must be compared with `equals`, not `==`.

options.why: Correct: boxing caches only small values (-128 to 127); larger ones are separate objects, so `==` compares references.
Small values are cached, but 1000 is not, so `==` is false for boxed 1000.

questions.explanation: This bites two sum and prefix-sum solutions that compare `map.get(x)` results with `==`. Compare with `equals` or unbox to int first.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `java.util.HashMap` are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A bucket with many colliding keys can be converted to a balanced tree once it grows past 8 entries and the table has 64 or more buckets.
options.why: Correct: treeification caps the worst-case lookup at O(log n) for Comparable keys.

options.text: It allows one `null` key and any number of null values.
options.why: Correct: unlike `Hashtable` or `ConcurrentHashMap`, `HashMap` accepts a null key.

options.text: Iteration returns entries in insertion order.
options.why: False: the order depends on bucket layout; use `LinkedHashMap` for insertion order.

options.text: It is safe to update from several threads without extra locking.
options.why: False: concurrent writes can corrupt it; use `ConcurrentHashMap`.

questions.explanation: Know the contracts: unordered, not thread safe, `null` friendly, O(1) expected and O(log n) in a treeified bin.
